t: That section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is amended by striking out “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(c), and 16” and inserting in lieu thereof “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(e), 14(d), 14(f), and 16”.

fable.w: This section is a purely technical amendment that replaces a list of cross-referenced section numbers in section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, rulemaking authority, or right to sue. A tempting reading is that section 12(i) concerns the allocation of regulatory powers and so implies rulemaking, but the text here only swaps statutory references and involves no outside party in any federal decision.

qwen_block.w: This section is a technical amendment to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, specifically updating the list of referenced sections within section 12(i). It does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards, or hearings. It merely changes statutory cross-references.
qwen_block.s: That section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is amended by striking out “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(c), and 16” and inserting in lieu thereof “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(e), 14(d), 14(f), and 16”.

opus.w: This section is a technical amendment that changes the list of sections cross-referenced in Section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act. It does not set up any comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking authority, consultation, or right to sue that brings parties outside the federal government into a decision. Reading in participation because Section 12(i) may involve agency rulemaking would mean relying on text that is not in this section.
opus.b:
**Step 1, reasoning.** One could read this as a "Yes" because Section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act lets the federal banking agencies administer and enforce the listed sections for banks, and that power may include rulemaking. That reading fails because the SECTION itself only swaps one list of cross-references for another. It does not require or authorize a comment period, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, consultation with outsiders, or a right to sue. Any role for outside parties would have to come from other provisions that are not shown here.

**Step 2, answer.**

qwen_chat.w: This section is a technical amendment that updates a list of referenced sections within the Securities Exchange Act. It does not create any new advisory committees, public comment periods, hearings, or consultation requirements. It merely changes which existing statutory sections are cited in section 12(i). Therefore, it does not involve participation by outside parties.
qwen_chat.s: That section 12(i) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is amended by striking out “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(c), and 16” and inserting in lieu thereof “sections 12, 13, 14(a), 14(e), 14(d), 14(f), and 16”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that amending the Securities Exchange Act to include new sections (like 14(e), 14(d), 14(f)) implicitly involves public participation because those sections might contain provisions for hearings or comments. However, the text provided *only* lists the section numbers being amended; it does not describe the content of those sections or establish any new participatory mechanisms itself. The section is purely a technical amendment to a cross-reference list.
